About the Office of Fair Trading

The Office of Fair Trading (OFT) was responsible for protecting consumer interests throughout the UK. It existed from 1973 to 1 April 2014.

About this page

This page reproduces examples of contract terms drawn from historic OFT enforcement work under the Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations 1999 (UTCCRs), together with revised wording adopted by businesses where available in response to OFT’s action. The examples were compiled to illustrate the practical effect of the UTCCRs, particularly the terms listed in Schedule 2 (commonly known as ‘the Grey List’).

The examples include terms challenged by the OFT at the time as potentially unfair. However, there was at no stage any finding in law as to the fairness or otherwise of any of the terms listed, only an administrative decision by the OFT that the original term appeared to raise concerns. Where action was taken by businesses in response to these concerns, it was decided at the time that no further enforcement action was warranted.

Since these examples were compiled, the UTCCRs and provisions of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (UCTA) which related to consumer contracts were replaced by Parts 1 and 2 of the Consumer Rights Act (CRA) 2015, which have been in force since 1 October 2015. In addition, the OFT closed and its responsibilities passed to a number of different organisations. This includes the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), which has primary responsibility for the enforcement of unfair contract terms legislation and for providing guidance for businesses in this area of law.

What this page is not

This page does not form part of the CMA’s unfair contract terms guidance. It should not be treated as a source of information about the CRA, or the CMA’s views on the interpretation and application of the CRA. The examples reflect historic OFT assessments under the UTCCRs and do not represent the CMA’s views on the fairness of any particular contract term.

Neither the original nor the reworked terms should be treated as definitively fair or unfair. Whether a term is fair depends on the circumstances of the individual case, including the other terms of the contract and the circumstances that existed when the contract was agreed.

Editing of the terms listed

The wording of the terms has been edited to make it easier for readers to understand why the OFT considered them fair or unfair. Unnecessary or repetitive wording has often been removed. In some cases, parts of a term have been omitted because the original term covered several different issues, while only one issue was relevant to the example being discussed. Where text has been left out, this is shown using an ellipsis (…).

Because a single term may consist of different elements that are unfair in different ways, parts of the same term may be found quoted in different places in the listing. Conversely, wording that covers a single issue for the purposes of Schedule 2, may be (for the business’s own reasons) broken up into different clauses or sub-clauses. In these cases, extracts from different parts of a contract may be quoted alongside one another in the listing.

Finally, the terms have also been edited to correct spelling and grammar to improve readability.

Organisation of the list

This page is arranged into 19 main sections.

The first 17 sections correspond to the 17 types of potentially unfair terms listed in Schedule 2 to the UTCCRs.

Section 18 consists of a number of terms that might be unfair in ways comparable to, but not directly covered by, Schedule 2.

Section 19 illustrates how the plain language requirement in Regulation 7 of the UTCCRs applies.

1. Excluding or restricting liability for death or personal injury

Schedule 2, paragraph 1, states that terms may be unfair if they have the object or effect of:

(a) excluding or limiting the legal liability of a seller or supplier in the event of the death of the consumer or personal injury to the latter resulting from the act or omission of that seller or supplier

Original term

All Star Soccer Schools … franchisees, their agents and their employees are not under any liability whatsoever in respect of personal injury, loss or damage howsoever caused whilst attending an All Star Soccer Schools’ course.

Action taken

New term: All Star Soccer Schools franchisees, their agents and their employees are insured against loss or injury through their negligence.

Original term

The use by the Member of any of the Company’s equipment or machinery or the facilities of any gymnasium owned by or occupied by the Company is entirely at the Member’s own risk.

Action taken

New term: In the absence of any negligence or other breach of duty by the Company the use by the Member of any of the Company’s equipment or machinery or the facilities of any gymnasium owned or occupied by the Company is entirely at the Member’s own risk.

Original term

We cannot accept any responsibility for the outcome of any contacts or meetings made through us, or for the accuracy of information supplied to us by members.

Action taken

New term: Initial Approach shall be under no obligation to provide Profiles which comply with all stated requirements of age, location, smoking preferences, etc, nor can it guarantee the outcome of any contacts or meetings.

Original term

Throughout the course of treatment … I will report any problems encountered to the clinic and make myself readily available to undergo such medical examination as shall be deemed necessary from the Physician. In the event of my failure to do this I shall fully and completely absolve the Physician and LST Clinic from all liability whatsoever.

Action taken

Term deleted.

Original term

Action taken

7. Supplier’s right to cancel without notice – paragraph 1(g) of Schedule 2

Schedule 2, paragraph 1, states that terms may be unfair if they have the object or effect of:

(g) enabling the seller or supplier to terminate a contract of indeterminate duration without reasonable notice except where there are serious grounds for doing so.

Original term

The right is specifically reserved … to terminate this engagement at any time, where in Bradleys Estate Agents’ opinion, the asking price is unrealistic in the light of the prevailing market conditions, … or the vendor later raises any additional point which is unacceptable to Bradleys Estate Agents.

Action taken

New term: We can end this agreement by giving 14 days’ notice in writing to you at any time in the following circumstances:

if we believe that the price at which you require to market the property is unrealistic: or

if you require us to take any step which may put us in breach of our legal or professional obligations.

Original term

This agreement and the agent’s Sole Selling Rights may only be terminated by the client upon 28 days written notice … the agent reserves the right to terminate this agreement without notice and any termination shall be without prejudice to any liability the client may have to pay commission and any other costs and charges.

Action taken

New term: Our agreement will continue until either you or we bring it to an end in writing and giving 14 days’ notice … any termination will not affect liability previously incurred by either of us to the other.
